biggest_risk: The dominant share of your savings sits inside registered accounts, so once the Registered Retirement Income Fund minimum withdrawals begin they would push taxable income steadily higher each year, regardless of what you actually need to spend.
best_lever: Choosing when and how quickly to draw down the registered balance, rather than waiting for the forced minimums to set the pace, is the lever that could most reshape your lifetime tax bill and what passes to your estate.
snapshot_intro: Your plan holds up across nearly every future the model tested, which earns the top grade. This result reflects thousands of tested scenarios, including severe crashes and prolonged inflation, but it cannot capture every possible risk such as legislative changes, major health issues, or divorce. With survival settled, the real question shifts from whether the money lasts to whether each dollar is working as hard as it could.
mirror_block: You are stepping into retirement now, with savings held mostly inside a registered account and a smaller amount in your tax-free account. Your guaranteed government income from the Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security has already begun, and it covers a large part of your planned spending. The portfolio fills the gap above that floor. The piece worth watching is how heavily your wealth leans on registered money, because that concentration would shape your taxes for years to come.
revenue_analysis: Your guaranteed income carries most of your planned lifestyle on its own, which means the portfolio is asked to cover only the remaining slice rather than the whole bill. That structure gives your spending a stable base that does not rise and fall with markets. Because the floor is lifelong and inflation-adjusted, the income you draw could stay steady even through difficult market stretches.
gov_explanation: Your Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security together form a guaranteed floor that arrives every month for life and is adjusted for inflation. Since these benefits have already started, there is no long bridge period where you would lean entirely on savings before government income kicks in, which is the harder phase for many retirees. That lifelong floor means the portfolio acts as a top-up rather than the main engine, easing how much weight your investments must carry.
longevity_analysis: The likely range of outcomes spans from a cautious path to a more favorable one, with half of all tested scenarios landing between those two bounds. The cautious end is not a worst case, simply the lower side of what is realistic given your savings and spending. Even on that cautious path, the balance holds up across the years the plan needs to cover, and hovering over the projection lets you trace where it sits at any age.
priority_actions: Your plan already works, so the question becomes how to make each dollar work harder. The annual cost embedded in your portfolio compounds quietly over the full length of retirement, and a lower-cost structure could redirect a meaningful sum back toward your own use or your estate. The order in which you draw accounts matters too, since pulling thoughtfully from the registered balance before the forced minimums arrive could smooth your taxable income and keep more of your tax-free room intact for later. With government income covering most of your needs, the surplus the portfolio represents could fund flexibility, whether that means richer early-retirement years or a buffer for the unexpected, without putting the plan at risk.
tax_analysis: Your effective tax rate today and the rate you would face in retirement sit close together, so the move into drawdown would not sharply change your tax picture on its own. The real pressure comes from the registered concentration, because the larger share of your savings lives in accounts that must convert to a Registered Retirement Income Fund and begin mandatory withdrawals. As those minimums grow with age, your taxable income could drift upward even in years you would rather draw less.
estate_analysis: On the median path your estate would leave a sizeable residual, with the cautious path still preserving a substantial sum. Your stated balanced preference fits this picture, since the plan neither drains the portfolio to nothing nor leaves it hoarded and untouched. The shape of what passes on would depend heavily on how much of it remains in registered form, which is fully taxable when settled.
obs_1: **Fee drag** : The yearly cost embedded in your portfolio adds up to a substantial sum over the full retirement horizon, the equivalent of handing several years of guaranteed government income to the management of your investments rather than keeping it for yourself.
obs_2: **Forced withdrawals** : Because the dominant share of your savings is registered, the mandatory minimums that begin in your early seventies would set a floor on what you must withdraw and report, climbing higher each year whether or not your spending does.
obs_3: **Estate tax split** : The registered portion of what you leave behind is fully taxable in the year it settles, while your tax-free account passes untouched, so the same estate could reach your heirs in very different net amounts depending on which account holds it.
obs_4: **Income floor** : Once your Canada Pension Plan and Old Age Security are both flowing, the guaranteed government income covers the larger part of your monthly spending target, leaving the portfolio responsible only for the remainder rather than the whole; because the benefits are already in payment, you sit in the steady-state phase rather than the earlier bridge phase that strains savings.
obs_5: **Rate stability** : Moving from working life into drawdown barely shifts your effective tax rate, so the tax conversation here is less about the rate itself and more about which accounts the income is forced to come from.
next_horizon: The data suggests the years just before and after the forced Registered Retirement Income Fund conversion could be the window where drawdown choices carry the most weight, since decisions made then would shape your taxable income for the rest of retirement. Adjusting the fee structure in that same stretch could compound in your favor over the years that remain. The next update of this assessment, in a year, would measure the effect of any such adjustments.
model_blind_spots: The model does not weigh a deliberate registered drawdown strategy in the years before the forced conversion, which for a profile this concentrated could meaningfully change the lifetime tax path. It also assumes today's government program rules hold, when future legislative changes to those benefits would land directly on a plan that leans this heavily on them. These dimensions could be explored in a future review.
efficiency_gap: Your plan works. Here is what it could look like if every dollar worked as hard as possible. The fee cost embedded in the portfolio quietly drains a sizeable sum over the retirement horizon, and a leaner structure could return much of that to your own use. The registered concentration also means a large slice of your estate would face tax when settled, where drawing down or converting more thoughtfully before the forced minimums could shrink that exposure. None of this changes whether the money lasts, only how much of it ends up working for you rather than for taxes and fees.
spending_flex: Your spending plan stays firm rather than flexing down when markets fall, which means the portfolio absorbs the full force of a bad stretch instead of sharing it. A plan that can trim withdrawals in lean years gives the portfolio room to recover, while a fixed draw asks the investments to deliver no matter the conditions. Because your guaranteed income already covers the larger part of your needs, this rigidity carries less sting than it would for someone leaning more on savings.
sequence_risk: The portfolio's likely range stretches from a cautious balance to a more favorable one, and which end you land near depends a great deal on the order in which returns arrive. Two retirees with identical savings and identical average returns can end up far apart simply because one met a downturn early, when withdrawals bite hardest into a shrinking balance, and the other met it late. The tornado chart ranks which inputs move your outcome most, showing where this timing risk sits relative to fees and spending.
strengths_risks: Your strengths stand out clearly: a lifelong government income floor that already covers the larger part of your spending, a plan that survives across nearly every tested future, and a withdrawal pace that sits within a sustainable band. The risks are more about efficiency than survival. The heavy tilt toward registered savings would push taxable income up as forced withdrawals climb, the annual fee load compounds against you over the full horizon, and a spending plan that does not flex leaves the portfolio to shoulder bad markets alone.
meltdown_analysis: Your planned spending already sits near the lower edge of what the model draws down, so there is limited additional room to trim before the cushion thins. That closeness suggests the target is well-matched to your resources, even as it means the slack on the spending side is slim.
